title.source: How can a monument connect belief, power and a wider landscape?

essentialQuestion.source: How can a monument connect belief, power and a wider landscape?

learningGoal.source: Explain a link between a great temple and the king who supported it, tell Angkor Wat apart from the wider Angkor site, and connect its first religious purpose with its later use and care.

evidence.question.source: The Khmer kingdom centred at Angkor, especially twelfth-century Angkor Wat; later Buddhist use and present-day Cambodia. Look at the towers first, then at what surrounds the temple.

read.sections.0.text.source:
A great building can show who had the resources to order it. A monument is a large structure that can honour or communicate something. It brings together labour, materials, knowledge and authority. Its layout may also express ideas about religion and the order of the world. So studying a monument means studying people and institutions, not only height or beauty.

Angkor Wat was built in the twelfth century under the Khmer king Suryavarman II. It was dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. Patronage means support for making or caring for art or buildings. The king's patronage of a great temple connected him with sacred authority. Sacred means having religious importance. The project also needed organised labour and specialist knowledge. The patron's role helps explain the project. But it does not name every worker, or tell us what everyone thought about the ruler.

Its five central towers stand for Mount Meru, a sacred mountain in Hindu and Buddhist traditions. Galleries and a moat (a wide channel of water around it) help make the building a picture of a universe. Stone reliefs tell Hindu stories, including the Churning of the Ocean of Milk. Buildings and images expressed ideas together. The photographs show the temple from a distance. Research supplies meanings that a view alone cannot show.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
A big building can show who had the money and power to order it. A monument is a large building with a meaning. It needs workers, materials, skill and power. Its shape can also show ideas about religion and the world.

Angkor Wat was built in the 1100s. The Khmer king Suryavarman II had it made. It was made for the Hindu god Vishnu. Patronage means paying for or supporting a building. The king's patronage linked him with sacred power. Sacred means holy. Many workers and experts built it. But we do not know all their names. We also do not know what everyone thought of the king.

Its five middle towers stand for Mount Meru. This is a holy mountain in Hindu and Buddhist stories. Walkways and a moat help the temple show a whole universe. A moat is a wide ditch of water around a building. Stone carvings tell Hindu stories. The photos show the temple from far away. Research tells us what a photo cannot.

read.sections.1.heading.source: A kingdom and a wider landscape

read.sections.1.text.source:
The Khmer kingdom was a state in the past whose centre and rulers changed. Angkor holds the remains of several capitals, one after another, not one building or one unchanging city. Its cultural links reached across Southeast Asia. Khmer builders adapted religious and building ideas linked with the Indian subcontinent, while developing their own local forms. Calling the site Cambodian today should not squeeze these centuries into the modern country's borders. Nor should it suggest that the builders simply copied a foreign model.

Angkor Wat belongs to this wider Angkor landscape. A landscape is an area shaped by nature and by people. UNESCO describes temples, routes, reservoirs, canals and other water structures. The monument stood in a lived-in setting with farming and transport, not alone among empty scenery. Sacred meanings and practical water management can belong to the same landscape. The moat does not need to have only one purpose.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
The Khmer kingdom lasted a long time. Its rulers and its capital changed. Angkor has the remains of several capitals, not just one city. The Khmer had links across Southeast Asia. Their builders used ideas from India. But they made their own local styles. Today Angkor is in Cambodia. But the old kingdom was not the same as the modern country. And its builders did not just copy others.

Angkor Wat is part of a bigger landscape. A landscape is land shaped by nature and by people. It has temples, roads, canals, lakes for storing water and other water works. People lived and farmed there. So the temple did not stand alone in empty land. The moat could be holy and useful at the same time.

read.sections.2.text.source:
The temple's use changed. Cambodia's APSARA National Authority describes how it became a Buddhist sacred place. Inscriptions from the sixteenth to the eighteenth centuries record pilgrims' acts of devotion, including visits by royalty. Some are written in languages other than Khmer. These records show later people actively making the temple meaningful, not simply receiving an unchanging object. This long process should not be reduced to one date when every part changed religion.

Angkor is still living heritage, with communities and religious practice alongside conservation. Conservation means careful, informed care for important places or objects. Caring for Angkor involves both the stones and the people connected with them. The stonework you see today has lasted through use, repair, research and care. A fuller explanation connects the temple's form with royal patronage, a working landscape and changing human meanings over time. A temple's history can go on long after its first patron is gone.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Later, the temple's use changed. It became a Buddhist holy place. Words carved in the stone tell of pilgrims who came to pray. Some of these visitors were royal. The words are from the 1500s to the 1700s. Some are in languages other than Khmer. They show that later people gave the temple new meaning. The change did not happen on one single date.

Today Angkor is living heritage. People live nearby and practise their religion there. Others work on conservation. Conservation means taking careful care of old places. The stones we see have lasted because people used, repaired and studied them. A temple's story goes on long after the king who had it made.

write.prompt.source: Explain one link between Angkor Wat and the society around it. Add a fact that the photos alone cannot show.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: One part of Angkor Wat is ...

write.example.source: One part of Angkor Wat is the wide moat around the temple. The reading tells us that Angkor had canals, lakes for storing water and other water works, and that people farmed and travelled there. This links the temple with a working landscape. It was not just a holy building standing alone. The moat could be sacred and useful at the same time. The photos show water, but not the whole system.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: Angkor Wat was first dedicated to Vishnu and is now a place of Buddhist practice. Teach Hindu and Buddhist ideas as traditions people hold. No learner is asked to share their religion or to take part in any practice.

educatorNotes.0.source: A building's present look and religious use are not necessarily the same as its first purpose, and a heritage landscape is not empty scenery. Keep Angkor Wat (one temple) apart from Angkor (the wider site of several capitals), and the Khmer kingdom apart from present-day Cambodia.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: royal patronage and sacred authority, the temple within a larger landscape of water and settlement, or its changing religious use and conservation. Don't accept a claim that the exact meaning of each tower can be seen without evidence from outside the photograph.

educatorNotes.2.source: Melody Rod-ari's Smarthistory essay supports the twelfth-century setting, Suryavarman II, Vishnu and the reading of patronage; exact dates and numbers of workers are left out on purpose, and its photographs are not used. UNESCO's Angkor page supports the water landscape and living heritage; don't repeat its outdated population numbers or general descriptions of residents.

educatorNotes.3.source: APSARA National Authority's page supports the change to Buddhist use and the sixteenth- to eighteenth-century pilgrim inscriptions. There is no single date when the whole temple changed religion.

educatorNotes.4.source: The two photographs are two views, not a before-and-after record of conservation. Scaffolding is visible on one tower in the 2009 photograph. That file is copyrighted and openly licensed (CC BY-SA 3.0), not public domain, and its photographer asks for the credit "Photo by CEphoto, Uwe Aranas" close to the image.
